evidence.title: Chronic expanding hematomas arising over a decade post primary total hip arthroplasty.
evidence.abstract: Background Chronic expanding hematoma (CEH) is an infrequent yet serious complication following total hip arthroplasty (THA). Mismanagement of this condition can result in severe consequences. The purpose of this study is to conduct a retrospective analysis of patients who developed CEH after THA at our institution over the past 20 years, complemented by a review of the existing literature. This comprehensive approach aims to contribute valuable clinical insights into the diagnosis and management of CEH. Methods In this study, we conducted a retrospective study of patients who had undergone THA within the past two decades and subsequently developed CEH during their follow-up period at our institution. The data collected encompassed fundamental patient demographics, including age, gender, and specifics regarding the primary THA implants. Additionally, we gathered preoperative, postoperative, and follow-up imaging studies. Following the data compilation, a thorough literature review was performed to aggregate and analyze the published cases of CEH occurring post-THA. Results Our follow-up data identified five patients who developed CEH more than ten years after undergoing THA. In one case, CEH manifested subsequent to a traumatic event, while the remaining four cases were non-traumatic. The outcomes following revision surgery were heterogeneous: two patients showed no indications of recurrence throughout a least follow-up period of over one year, one patient eventually underwent amputation, and two patients developed periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), an ongoing management challenge. Our literature review revealed nine previously reported cases with similar clinical features. A summary is as follows: Etiology : While often linked to trauma or surgery, a definitive cause is not always present. evidence.title: Powered Versus Manual Acetabular Component Extraction in Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Comprehensive Analysis of 98 Cases.
evidence.abstract: Background Revision total hip arthroplasty (R-THA) often requires removal of well-fixed acetabular components, where minimizing bone loss and operative time are critical. While manual extraction tools have been the traditional approach, powered systems device may improve efficiency, yet comparative clinical data remain limited. Methods We performed a retrospective review of 98 R-THAs (32 powered, 66 manual) from an institutional database (2021-2024). Patient demographics, operative characteristics, extraction times, and healthcare utilization outcomes (length of stay [LOS], discharge disposition, 90-day readmission, 90-day complications, and 1-year reoperations) were analyzed using nonparametric and categorical statistical tests. Results Baseline characteristics were similar across groups. Cup sizes removed and reimplanted were largely comparable between groups, indicating minimal differences in bone preservation. Time to cup removal was significantly shorter with the powered device, with 82% completed in ≤10 minutes and none exceeding 20 minutes, compared with the manual group where 58% required 5 to 10 minutes, 33% required 10 to 20 minutes, and 8% exceeded 20 minutes (p Conclusion The use of the powered acetabular extraction system was associated with significantly reduced extraction times compared with a manual extraction device in R-THA. One-year reoperation rates were comparable, as were complication/readmission rates and replacement cup sizes. These findings highlight the efficiency benefits of powered explantation as well as its safety. Level of evidence Level III (Retrospective comparative cohort study). See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

evidence.title: Phase 1 study of the pharmacokinetics and clinical proof-of-concept activity of a biofilm-disrupting human monoclonal antibody in patients with chronic prosthetic joint infection of the knee or hip.
evidence.abstract: We report the results of a first-in-human phase 1 clinical study to evaluate TRL1068, a native human monoclonal antibody that disrupts bacterial biofilms with broad-spectrum activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative species. The study population consisted of patients with chronic periprosthetic joint infections (PJIs) of the knee or hip, including both monomicrobial and polymicrobial infections, that are highly resistant to antibiotics due to biofilm formation. TRL1068 was administered via a single pre-surgical intravenous infusion in three sequentially ascending dose groups (6, 15, and 30 mg/kg). Concomitant perioperative antibiotics were pathogen-targeted as prescribed by the treating physician. In this double-blinded study, 4 patients were randomized to receive placebo and 11 patients to receive TRL1068 on day 1, as well as targeted antibiotics for 7 days prior to the scheduled removal of the infected implant and placement of an antibiotic-eluting spacer as the first stage of the standard of care two-stage exchange arthroplasty. No adverse events attributable to TRL1068 were reported. TRL1068 serum half-life was 15-18 days. At day 8, the concentration in synovial fluid was approximately 60% of the blood level and thus at least 15-fold above the threshold for biofilm-disrupting activity in vitro . Explanted prostheses were sonicated to release adherent bacteria for culture, with elimination of the implant bacteria observed in 3 of the 11 patients who received TRL1068, which compares favorably to prior PJI treatments. None of the patients who received TRL1068 had a relapse of the original infection by the end of the study (day 169). Clinical trials This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT04763759.

evidence.title: Investigation of the In Vivo Performance of Metal-on-Metal Motec Total Wrist Arthroplasty-An Explant Analysis.
evidence.abstract: Background Despite the Motec metal-on-metal (MoM) total wrist arthroplasty (TWA) being among the most implanted and most reported implants, there remains concern about the articulation following the issues in hips, where early wear led to catastrophic failure. Materials and Methods Explant analysis was undertaken on seven MoM Motec wrists, explanted for technical issues in the first 3 years postimplantation, at the macro-, micro-, and nanoscales. Results Compared with unworn Motec implants, five of the explanted heads and five of the cups became smoother in vivo. The articulating surfaces of every explanted component had negative skewness. The articulating surfaces of the components did not show any of the major damage associated with hip implants but did demonstrate multidirectional scratches and dark marks mainly situated toward their equator. Four explants showed indentation marks on the rims of their cups and necks from component impingement. The nano- and macroscale observations suggested abrasive wear to be the dominant wear mechanism. Most components demonstrated evidence of self-polishing. Conclusion In the short term, the MoM Motec TWA does not seem to be affected by the wear issues seen in failing MoM total hip replacements with all of the explanted Motec components remaining within manufacturing tolerances.

evidence.title: Gross Taper Failure and Fracture of the True Neck in Total Hip Arthroplasty: Retrieval Scanning Electron Microscope Analysis.
evidence.abstract: Background and objectives : wear and corrosion can lead to the gross failure of the Morse taper junction with the consequent fracture of the true neck of the prosthetic stem in hip arthroplasty. Materials and Methods : 58-year-old male patient, with a BMI of 38 kg/m 2 . Because of avascular necrosis, in 2007, a metal-on-metal total hip arthroplasty was implanted in him, with a TMZF stem and a Co-Cr head. In December 2020, he complained of acute left hip pain associated with the deterioration of his left leg and total functional impairment, preceded by the crunching of the hip. X-rays and CT scan showed a fracture of the prosthetic neck that necessitated prosthetic revision surgery. A Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) analysis of the retrieved prosthetic components was conducted. Results : Macroscopically, the trunnion showed a typical bird beak appearance, due to a massive material loss of about half of its volume. The gross material loss apparently due to abrasion extended beyond the trunnion to the point of failure on the true neck about half a centimeter distal from the taper. SEM analysis demonstrated fatigue rupture modes, and the crack began close to the neck's surface. On the lateral surface, several scratches were found, suggesting an intense wear that could be due to abrasion. Conclusions : The analysis we conducted on the explanted THA showed a ductile rupture, began close to the upper surface of the prosthetic neck where the presence of many scratches had concentrated stresses and led to a fatigue fracture.

Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: Derivative and predictive controllers for venous-aware regulation
informational.lesson: Derivative-based controllers are too sensitive to noise. Predictive models require accurate forward models that don't exist for CSF dynamics.
Any anti-fouling mechanism that relies on flow direction must be tested against RETROGRADE flow. Retrograde flow is a realistic clinical scenario (cough, Valsalva, venous pressure changes).

ALWAYS report worst-case reliability for clinical devices. Averages mask catastrophic failure modes. Thermal activation in a 37°C body environment has a narrow window (37-45°C = 8°C max). Sensor electronics are a SPOF that cannot be fully resolved by redundancy (common-mode failures).

informational.mechanism: M5_REFINED adaptive over-drainage controller (sleep-state + venous pressure)
informational.lesson: Do not assume VP shunt problems apply to the eShunt. The eShunt's drainage geometry is fundamentally different (short path, no siphon). Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry. Over-drainage is siphon-driven; without a hydrostatic column, it may not occur.

Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

The purpose of this study is to conduct a retrospective analysis of patients who developed CEH after THA at our institution over the past 20 years, complemented by a review of the existing literature. This comprehensive approach aims to contribute valuable clinical insights into the diagnosis and management of CEH. Methods In this study, we conducted a retrospective study of patients who had undergone THA within the past two decades and subsequently developed CEH during their follow-up period at our institution. Following the data compilation, a thorough literature review was performed to aggregate and analyze the published cases of CEH occurring post-THA. Results Our follow-up data identified five patients who developed CEH more than ten years after undergoing THA. custody_records.raw_content: Background Revision total hip arthroplasty (R-THA) often requires removal of well-fixed acetabular components, where minimizing bone loss and operative time are critical. While manual extraction tools have been the traditional approach, powered systems device may improve efficiency, yet comparative clinical data remain limited. Methods We performed a retrospective review of 98 R-THAs (32 powered, 66 manual) from an institutional database (2021-2024). Patient demographics, operative characteristics, extraction times, and healthcare utilization outcomes (length of stay [LOS], discharge disposition, 90-day readmission, 90-day complications, and 1-year reoperations) were analyzed using nonparametric and categorical statistical tests. Results Baseline characteristics were similar across groups. Cup sizes removed and reimplanted were largely comparable between groups, indicating minimal differences in bone preservation. Time to cup removal was significantly shorter with the powered device, with 82% completed in ≤10 minutes and none exceeding 20 minutes, compared with the manual group where 58% required 5 to 10 minutes, 33% required 10 to 20 minutes, and 8% exceeded 20 minutes (p Conclusion The use of the powered acetabular extraction system was associated with significantly reduced extraction times compared with a manual extraction device in R-THA. One-year reoperation rates were comparable, as were complication/readmission rates and replacement cup sizes. These findings highlight the efficiency benefits of powered explantation as well as its safety. Level of evidence Level III (Retrospective comparative cohort study). See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

custody_records.raw_content: We report the results of a first-in-human phase 1 clinical study to evaluate TRL1068, a native human monoclonal antibody that disrupts bacterial biofilms with broad-spectrum activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative species. The study population consisted of patients with chronic periprosthetic joint infections (PJIs) of the knee or hip, including both monomicrobial and polymicrobial infections, that are highly resistant to antibiotics due to biofilm formation. TRL1068 was administered via a single pre-surgical intravenous infusion in three sequentially ascending dose groups (6, 15, and 30 mg/kg). Concomitant perioperative antibiotics were pathogen-targeted as prescribed by the treating physician. In this double-blinded study, 4 patients were randomized to receive placebo and 11 patients to receive TRL1068 on day 1, as well as targeted antibiotics for 7 days prior to the scheduled removal of the infected implant and placement of an antibiotic-eluting spacer as the first stage of the standard of care two-stage exchange arthroplasty. No adverse events attributable to TRL1068 were reported. TRL1068 serum half-life was 15-18 days. At day 8, the concentration in synovial fluid was approximately 60% of the blood level and thus at least 15-fold above the threshold for biofilm-disrupting activity in vitro . Explanted prostheses were sonicated to release adherent bacteria for culture, with elimination of the implant bacteria observed in 3 of the 11 patients who received TRL1068, which compares favorably to prior PJI treatments. None of the patients who received TRL1068 had a relapse of the original infection by the end of the study (day 169). Clinical trials This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT04763759.

custody_records.raw_content: Background Despite the Motec metal-on-metal (MoM) total wrist arthroplasty (TWA) being among the most implanted and most reported implants, there remains concern about the articulation following the issues in hips, where early wear led to catastrophic failure. Materials and Methods Explant analysis was undertaken on seven MoM Motec wrists, explanted for technical issues in the first 3 years postimplantation, at the macro-, micro-, and nanoscales. Results Compared with unworn Motec implants, five of the explanted heads and five of the cups became smoother in vivo. The articulating surfaces of every explanted component had negative skewness. The articulating surfaces of the components did not show any of the major damage associated with hip implants but did demonstrate multidirectional scratches and dark marks mainly situated toward their equator. Four explants showed indentation marks on the rims of their cups and necks from component impingement. The nano- and macroscale observations suggested abrasive wear to be the dominant wear mechanism. Most components demonstrated evidence of self-polishing. Conclusion In the short term, the MoM Motec TWA does not seem to be affected by the wear issues seen in failing MoM total hip replacements with all of the explanted Motec components remaining within manufacturing tolerances.

custody_records.raw_content: Background and objectives : wear and corrosion can lead to the gross failure of the Morse taper junction with the consequent fracture of the true neck of the prosthetic stem in hip arthroplasty. Materials and Methods : 58-year-old male patient, with a BMI of 38 kg/m 2 . Because of avascular necrosis, in 2007, a metal-on-metal total hip arthroplasty was implanted in him, with a TMZF stem and a Co-Cr head. In December 2020, he complained of acute left hip pain associated with the deterioration of his left leg and total functional impairment, preceded by the crunching of the hip. X-rays and CT scan showed a fracture of the prosthetic neck that necessitated prosthetic revision surgery. A Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) analysis of the retrieved prosthetic components was conducted. Results : Macroscopically, the trunnion showed a typical bird beak appearance, due to a massive material loss of about half of its volume. The gross material loss apparently due to abrasion extended beyond the trunnion to the point of failure on the true neck about half a centimeter distal from the taper. SEM analysis demonstrated fatigue rupture modes, and the crack began close to the neck's surface. On the lateral surface, several scratches were found, suggesting an intense wear that could be due to abrasion. Conclusions : The analysis we conducted on the explanted THA showed a ductile rupture, began close to the upper surface of the prosthetic neck where the presence of many scratches had concentrated stresses and led to a fatigue fracture.
